blocks.text: When heat is added to a system there is an increase in the internal energy due to the rise in temperature, an increase in pressure or a change in the state. If at the same time a substance is allowed to do work on its environment by expansion, the heat Q required will be the heat necessary to change the internal energy of the substance from U1 in the first state to U2 in the second state plus the work W done on the environment: Q = (U2 - U1) + W, or Q = delta U + W ... (6.5). Thus the change in internal energy delta U = U2 - U1 is defined as Q - W. Since it is the same for all processes concerning the state, the first law can be stated as:

blocks.title: First law of thermodynamics
blocks.text: In any thermodynamic process, when heat Q is added to a system, this energy appears as an increase in the internal energy delta U stored in the system plus the work W done by the system on its surroundings.

items: Conservation principle: the underlying principle of the first law is the conservation of energy. It asserts that while energy can change from one form to another (such as from chemical potential energy to thermal energy), the total amount of energy in an isolated system remains constant over time.

Wider applicability: beyond mechanical systems the first law applies universally to all forms of energy and all types of processes, including chemical reactions, electrical systems and nuclear reactions; it provides a foundational understanding that allows scientists and engineers to predict and understand energy transformations in various contexts.

blocks.text: The first law expresses the law of conservation of energy by affirming that energy is a conserved quantity in isolated systems; it provides a framework to understand how energy is transferred and transformed within systems without violating the principle that energy cannot be created nor destroyed. Sign conventions (For Your Information): heat into the system +Q, heat out of the system -Q, work done on the system -W, work done by the system +W.

A bicycle pump is a good example: when we pump on the handle rapidly it becomes hot due to the mechanical work done on the gas, raising its internal energy. In the arrangement of Fig. 6.6 a bicycle pump has a blocked outlet; a thermocouple connected through the blocked outlet allows the air temperature to be monitored. When the piston is rapidly pushed, the thermometer shows a temperature rise due to the increase of internal energy of the air: the push force does work on the air, increasing its internal energy, which is shown by the rise in temperature of the air. Human metabolism also provides an example of energy conservation: human beings and other animals do work when they walk, run or move; work requires energy, and energy is also needed for growth, to make new cells and to replace old cells that have died. The energy-transforming processes within an organism are called metabolism. Applying the first law (delta U = Q - W) to an organism such as the human body, work done results in a decrease in internal energy of the body; consequently the body temperature, or in other words the internal energy, is maintained by the food we eat.

blocks.title: Example 6.2
blocks.text: A gas is enclosed in a container fitted with a piston of cross-sectional area 0.10 m^2; the pressure of the gas is maintained at 8000 N m^-2. When heat is slowly transferred, the piston is pushed up through a distance of 4.0 cm. If 42 J of heat is transferred to the system during the expansion, what is the change in internal energy of the system? Solution: the work done by the gas is W = P delta V = P A delta y = 8000 N m^-2 x 0.10 m^2 x 4.0 x 10^-2 m = 32 N m = 32 J. The change in internal energy follows from the first law: delta U = Q - W = 42 J - 32 J = 10 J.

blocks.caption: The first law of thermodynamics, isothermal and adiabatic processes, reversibility (original diagram after Figures 6.6 and 6.7 and topics 6.4 and 6.5).
blocks.long_description: Heat added to a system goes partly into raising its internal energy and partly into work the system does on its surroundings, with heat in and work out counted positive; the law is the conservation of energy and applies to every kind of process, as a bicycle pump warming when its piston is pushed and a body fed by food both show. In an isothermal change the temperature and so the internal energy of an ideal gas stay fixed, all the heat supplied becomes work, the change must be slow, and the P-V curve is a hyperbola called an isotherm. In an adiabatic change no heat is exchanged, work is done at the expense of internal energy so the temperature falls on expansion and rises on compression, the change is rapid or insulated, and the steeper P-V curve is an adiabat. A reversible process can be retraced exactly leaving no change in the surroundings, as slow compression nearly can; sudden changes, friction and dissipation make a process irreversible.

blocks.text: An isothermal process is carried out at constant temperature, so the condition for applying Boyle's law to the gas is fulfilled: when a gas expands or compresses isothermally, the product of its pressure and volume remains constant. If P1, V1 are the initial pressure and volume and P2, V2 those after the isothermal change (Fig. 6.7a), P1 V1 = P2 V2. For an ideal gas the PE associated with its molecules is zero, so the internal energy depends only on its temperature, which here remains constant; therefore delta U = 0 and the first law reduces to Q = W. Thus if a gas expands and does external work W, an amount of heat Q has to be supplied to the gas to produce an isothermal change. Since the transfer of heat from one place to another requires time, to keep the temperature constant the expansion or compression must take place slowly. The curve representing an isothermal process is an isotherm. (Brain Teaser: why does the internal energy of an ideal gas remain constant during isothermal expansion? Because it depends on temperature alone.)

An adiabatic process is one in which no heat enters or leaves the system; therefore Q = 0 and the first law gives W = -delta U. Thus if the gas expands and does external work, it is done at the expense of the internal energy of its molecules and the temperature of the gas falls; conversely an adiabatic compression causes the temperature of the gas to rise because of the work done on the gas. Adiabatic change occurs when the gas expands or is compressed rapidly, particularly when the gas is contained in an insulated cylinder. Examples of adiabatic processes: the rapid escape of air from a burst tyre; the rapid expansion and compression of air through which a sound wave is passing; cloud formation in the atmosphere. As the temperature of the gas does not remain constant, P V^gamma = constant, where gamma is the ratio of the molar specific heat of the gas at constant pressure to the molar specific heat at constant volume. The curve representing an adiabatic process is an adiabat (Fig. 6.7b), steeper than the isotherm.

blocks.caption: Isothermal against adiabatic
rows: falls on expansion, rises on compression

blocks.prompt: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 300 J of work; find its change in internal energy (numerical 6.3). Why is an adiabat steeper than an isotherm, and what happens to the temperature and pressure of a gas expanding adiabatically (short question 6.6; constructed response 6.3)?
blocks.explanation: delta U = Q - W = 500 - 300 = 200 J. In an adiabatic expansion the pressure falls both because the volume grows and because the temperature drops, whereas in an isothermal expansion only the volume effect acts, so the adiabat falls faster: P V^gamma with gamma greater than 1 against PV. Expanding adiabatically the gas does work from its own internal energy, so its temperature falls and its pressure falls more steeply than for an isothermal change.

items: First law: Q = delta U + W; heat in +Q, out -Q; work by +W, on -W; conservation of energy for every process (bicycle pump warms when pushed; the body's internal energy is kept up by food). Example 6.2: W = 32 J, delta U = 10 J.

Isothermal: T constant, PV = constant, delta U = 0, Q = W, slow, isotherm. Adiabatic: Q = 0, W = -delta U, P V^gamma = constant, rapid or insulated (burst tyre, sound wave, cloud formation), adiabat steeper.
